topics.name: Adding Two-Digit Numbers
topics.summary: Adding the tens, adding the ones, and putting them together.

objectives.text: Say how many tens and how many ones are in a number.
Build a number from bundles of ten and single ones.
Say which of two numbers is bigger by looking at the tens first.

keyTerms.definition: A bundle of ten single things, held together as one group.
A single thing, not in a bundle.
A number written with two figures, like 34 or 70.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body:
You will learn why 34 is not just "three and four".

You will learn to see numbers as tens and ones.

This makes big numbers much easier.

sections.heading: Counting one by one is slow
sections.body:
Imagine 34 seeds on the ground.

You could count them one by one. 1, 2, 3, 4 ... 34.

That works. But it takes a long time. And it is easy to lose your place.

There is a faster way.

Put the seeds into bundles of ten.

sections.heading: Bundles of ten
sections.body:
Count out ten seeds. Tie them together. That is one bundle.

Do it again. And again.

With 34 seeds you get:

    bundle   bundle   bundle      and  4 loose seeds
      10   +   10   +   10     +         4      = 34

So 34 is three tens and four ones.

Now look at how we write it:

    3 4
    | |
    | └── the ones: 4
    └──── the tens: 3

The left figure counts the bundles. The right figure counts the loose ones.
sections.example:
What is 58 made of?

Look at the two figures.

    5 is on the left → 5 bundles of ten → 50
    8 is on the right → 8 loose ones → 8

So 58 is five tens and eight ones.

    50 + 8 = 58

Now the other way round. Build 70.

    7 bundles of ten = 70
    0 loose ones = 0

So 70 is seven tens and NO ones. The 0 is not nothing — it is telling you there are no loose ones left over.

sections.heading: Comparing is faster with tens
sections.body:
Which is bigger, 43 or 38?

Do not count them all. Look at the tens first.

    43 has 4 tens.
    38 has 3 tens.

4 bundles is more than 3 bundles.

So 43 is bigger. You did not even need to look at the ones.

Only if the tens are the SAME do you look at the ones. Like 45 and 42: both have 4 tens, so compare 5 and 2. 45 is bigger.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. How many tens and how many ones are in 26?

2. How many tens and how many ones are in 90?

3. I have 6 bundles of ten and 3 loose seeds. What number do I have?

4. Which is bigger, 52 or 49? Look at the tens first.

5. Which is bigger, 61 or 67? Careful — the tens are the same.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Ten single things make one bundle of ten.
• In a two-digit number, the left figure counts tens and the right figure counts ones.
• 34 means three tens and four ones.
• A 0 in the ones place means no loose ones left over.
• To compare, look at the tens first.

objectives.text: Add two two-digit numbers by adding tens and ones separately.
Know when ten ones must be traded for one ten.
Check whether an answer is sensible.

keyTerms.definition: To put two groups together and find how many there are altogether.
The whole amount after you put the groups together.
To swap ten loose ones for one bundle of ten.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body:
You will learn to add numbers like 23 + 45.

The trick is to add the tens and the ones separately.

Then you put the two answers together.

sections.heading: Add the tens, add the ones
sections.body:
Take 23 + 45.

Break each number into tens and ones:

    23  is  2 tens  and  3 ones
    45  is  4 tens  and  5 ones

Now add the tens:   2 tens + 4 tens = 6 tens = 60
Now add the ones:   3 ones + 5 ones = 8 ones = 8

Put them together:  60 + 8 = 68

So 23 + 45 = 68.

You never had to count past ten. You just added 2 and 4, then 3 and 5.
sections.example:
A market stall.

A trader sells 31 oranges in the morning and 26 oranges in the afternoon. How many did she sell altogether?

Break them up:

    31  is  3 tens and 1 one
    26  is  2 tens and 6 ones

Tens:  3 + 2 = 5 tens = 50
Ones:  1 + 6 = 7 ones = 7

Altogether: 50 + 7 = 57 oranges.

Is that sensible? She sold about 30 and about 26. Together that should be a bit under 60. 57 is a bit under 60. Good.

sections.heading: When the ones make ten or more
sections.body:
Sometimes the ones add up to ten or more.

Take 28 + 15.

    Tens:  2 + 1 = 3 tens = 30
    Ones:  8 + 5 = 13 ones

13 ones is too many to leave loose. Ten of them make a bundle.

    13 ones = 1 ten and 3 ones

So now you have:

    3 tens + 1 more ten = 4 tens = 40
    and 3 ones left over

    40 + 3 = 43

So 28 + 15 = 43.

That swap — ten loose ones becoming one bundle — is called trading.

sections.heading: Check if your answer is sensible
sections.body:
Always look at your answer and ask: could that be right?

If you add 28 + 15 and get 33, something is wrong. 28 + 15 must be more than 28 + 10, which is 38. So 33 is too small.

If you get 413, that is far too big. You were adding two numbers smaller than 30 each.

A sensible answer for 28 + 15 is somewhere in the forties. 43 fits.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. 14 + 23

2. 40 + 35

3. 26 + 12

4. 17 + 15  (careful — the ones make more than ten)

5. A boy picks 22 mangoes on Monday and 19 on Tuesday. How many altogether?

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Break each number into tens and ones.
• Add the tens. Add the ones. Put them together.
• If the ones reach ten or more, trade ten ones for one ten.
• Always check that your answer looks sensible.

questions.question: How many tens are in the number 47?
questions.explanation: The figure on the LEFT counts the bundles of ten. In 47 that is the 4, so there are 4 tens. If you chose 7, you looked at the ones instead — the 7 counts the loose ones.

questions.question: I have 6 bundles of ten and 3 loose seeds. What number do I have?
questions.explanation: The tens go on the left and the ones on the right. 6 tens and 3 ones is written 63. If you chose 36, you swapped them round — that would be 3 tens and 6 ones, a much smaller number.

questions.question: Which number is bigger, 52 or 49?
options: You need to count them all
questions.explanation: Look at the tens first. 52 has 5 tens and 49 has 4 tens. 5 bundles is more than 4 bundles, so 52 is bigger. You did not even need to look at the ones. The 9 in 49 is bigger than the 2, but ones only matter when the tens are the same.

questions.question: What is 23 + 45?
questions.explanation: Add the tens: 2 + 4 = 6 tens, which is 60. Add the ones: 3 + 5 = 8. Put them together: 60 + 8 = 68.

questions.question: What is 28 + 15?
questions.explanation: The ones make more than ten here. Tens: 2 + 1 = 3 tens (30). Ones: 8 + 5 = 13, which is 1 more ten and 3 ones. So 30 + 10 = 40, plus 3 = 43. If you chose 313, you wrote the tens and the ones side by side instead of trading.

questions.question: A trader sells 31 oranges in the morning and 26 in the afternoon. How many altogether?
questions.explanation: Tens: 3 + 2 = 5 tens (50). Ones: 1 + 6 = 7. Together that is 57. Check it is sensible: about 30 plus about 26 should be a bit under 60, and 57 is.
